title: Higher-Order Components with TypeScript
description: Learn to type higher-order components (HOCs) properly so the wrapped component retains full prop inference.

data.text: A **higher-order component (HOC)** is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with additional props or behavior. Typing HOCs correctly is one of the more advanced TypeScript challenges in React — get it wrong and the wrapped component loses all its prop types.

HOCs are functions with this signature: `(WrappedComponent: ComponentType<Props>) => ComponentType<EnhancedProps>`. The enhanced component receives everything the original component needed plus whatever the HOC adds. The trick is making sure TypeScript tracks both sides of that equation.

terms.definition: A function that accepts a component and returns a new component with enhanced capabilities.

Constructs a type by picking all properties from P except those in K. Used to remove props the HOC provides itself.
Pattern where TypeScript extracts the wrapped component's original prop types and combines them with HOC-injected props.

data.text: The simplest case: an HOC that injects a single prop. The consumer provides the remaining props, and TypeScript tracks which ones come from the HOC and which are left for the consumer.

data.text: Real applications compose multiple HOCs: one for authentication, one for data fetching, one for logging. Each HOC must preserve the prop types of what came before it. The `Omit` pattern ensures each HOC removes only the props it provides.

data.title: Static Properties Are Lost
data.text: HOCs do not automatically copy static properties like displayName, propTypes, or defaultProps from the wrapped component. Use a utility like hoist-non-react-statics to preserve them.

data.title: Exercise: withLoading HOC
data.description: Build a withLoading HOC that injects an isLoading boolean prop. The HOC should accept a WrappedComponent that needs { isLoading: boolean } plus its own props. The consumer should never provide isLoading — it is computed inside the HOC from a useLoadingState hook.
steps: Define LoadingProps interface with isLoading: boolean

Build withLoading

that returns a component with Omit
Inside the HOC, use a loading state and pass isLoading to the wrapped component
Wrap a UserCard component that displays loading spinner when isLoading is true
Verify TypeScript prevents passing isLoading to the enhanced component
data.expectedOutcome: A withLoading HOC where the wrapped component receives isLoading automatically, and TypeScript shows an error if a consumer tries to pass isLoading manually.

items.question: Are HOCs still used in modern React?
items.answer: Less commonly now that hooks exist, but they are still relevant for class component codebases, cross-cutting concerns in shared libraries, and certain patterns like theming providers.

items.question: Why not use intersection types instead of Omit?
items.answer: Intersection types (P & InjectedProps) work for the wrapped component's input but don't help the consumer. Omit<P, keyof InjectedProps> is what removes injected props from the consumer-facing API.

items.question: Can an HOC add event handlers or refs?
items.answer: Yes. Use the same pattern: define the injected props in an interface, add them inside the wrapper, and omit them from the consumer. For refs, use forwardRef in the wrapped component.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: HOCs wrap components with additional props and behavior
P extends object keeps the generic type safe
Omit<P, keyof InjectedProps> removes HOC props from consumer

ComponentType

accepts both function and class components
Compose HOCs by chaining — each removes its own injected props
data.takeaway: Correctly typed HOCs let you compose behaviors while keeping every prop fully inferable for the consumer.
